title: 3.1–3.3 Catch-Up
contentObjective: I can show I am caught up on Lessons 3.1–3.3 by using each lesson's big idea in mixed practice.
languageObjective: I can explain which lesson's big idea I used and how, using key vocabulary from Lessons 3.1–3.3.

revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Which Brand to Buy?
revealWordProblem.text: Deon needs to buy dishwasher detergent. He finds these two brands at the store: Shine costs $5.40 and is good for 18 loads, and Pure costs $6.30 and is good for 21 loads. Which brand is the better buy per load, and which brand should he buy?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: Shine costs $5.40 ÷ 18 loads = $0.30 per load. Pure costs $6.30 ÷ 21 loads = $0.30 per load. Both brands cost exactly the same amount per load, so they are equally good buys — Deon can pick either brand.

vocabulary.definition: Use a ratio to compare two quantities by division.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Usar una razón para comparar dos cantidades mediante la división.
vocabulary.visual: 3 red tiles to 5 blue tiles can be written 3:5 or 3/5.
vocabulary.cloze: A comparison of two quantities by division is a ___.

examples.why: It compares two quantities.
One amount alone compares nothing.

vocabulary.definition: A way to compare two amounts, like 3 to 2.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una manera de comparar dos cantidades, como 3 a 2.
vocabulary.cloze: A comparison of two quantities, like 3 to 5, is a ___.

examples.why: It compares two quantities.
A single number does not compare two quantities.

vocabulary.definition: Looking at two or more amounts to see how they are related.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Mirar dos o más cantidades para ver cómo se relacionan.
vocabulary.visual: 5 eggs vs. 3 eggs — which recipe uses more?
vocabulary.cloze: Showing how two amounts relate to each other is a ___.

examples.why: It looks at two amounts to see how they relate.
It states a single amount without relating it to anything.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing one part of a group to another part.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una razón que compara una parte de un grupo con otra parte.
vocabulary.visual: 3 cups flour : 2 cups sugar (ingredient to ingredient)
vocabulary.cloze: A ratio that compares one part of a group to another part is a ___ ratio.

examples.why: It compares one part to another part.
That compares a part to the whole.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing one part to the whole group.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una razón que compara una parte con todo el grupo.
vocabulary.visual: 3 cups flour out of 5 cups total → 3:5
vocabulary.cloze: A ratio that compares one part of a group to the total is a ___ ratio.

examples.why: It compares a part to the whole group.
That compares a part to another part.

vocabulary.definition: Writing a ratio with two dots between the numbers, like 3:2.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Escribir una razón con dos puntos entre los números, como 3:2.
vocabulary.cloze: Writing a ratio with a colon, like 3:5, is using ___.

examples.why: It uses a colon between the two numbers being compared.
It uses words instead of a colon, so it is not colon notation.

vocabulary.definition: A bar cut into equal parts that shows how two amounts in a ratio compare, and how they make up the whole.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una barra dividida en partes iguales que muestra cómo se comparan dos cantidades de una razón y cómo forman el total.
vocabulary.visual: 3 equal parts of apple juice beside 2 equal parts of sparkling water — 5 parts of fruit drink in all.
vocabulary.cloze: A bar cut into equal parts that shows how a ratio breaks apart is a ___ ___.

examples.text: 3 shaded parts beside 2 unshaded parts for a 3:2 recipe
examples.why: Equal, labelled parts model both amounts and the whole.

examples.text: A bar with parts of different sizes and no labels
examples.why: Unequal, unlabelled parts cannot show a ratio.

vocabulary.definition: Two number lines lined up so matching tick marks show the two quantities in a ratio at the same time.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Dos rectas numéricas alineadas para que las marcas correspondientes muestren las dos cantidades de una razón al mismo tiempo.
vocabulary.visual: Cups of apple juice 0, 3, 6, 12 above cups of fruit drink 0, 5, 10, 20.
vocabulary.cloze: Two lines whose matching ticks pair the two amounts in a ratio form a ___ ___ ___.

examples.text: Cups of juice on one line, cups of drink on the other, ticks aligned
examples.why: Matching positions pair the two quantities.

examples.text: One line showing only cups of drink
examples.why: There is no second quantity to pair against.

vocabulary.definition: A rate compares different units; a unit rate compares a quantity to 1 unit.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una tasa compara unidades diferentes; una tasa unitaria compara una cantidad con 1 unidad.
vocabulary.visual: 180 miles in 3 hours = 60 miles per 1 hour.
vocabulary.cloze: A rate compares different units; a ___ ___ compares a quantity to exactly 1 unit.

examples.why: It gives the amount for one unit.
A rate, but not yet per one.

vocabulary.definition: Tables that organize pairs of equivalent ratios.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Tablas que organizan pares de razones equivalentes.
vocabulary.visual: 2:3, 4:6, and 6:9 belong in the same ratio table.
vocabulary.cloze: A table whose every row holds the same comparison is a ___ ___.

examples.why: Each row scales both parts equally.
The last row was not scaled.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio comparing two amounts with different units, like miles per hour.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una razón que compara dos cantidades con unidades distintas, como millas por hora.
vocabulary.cloze: A ratio that compares two quantities with different units is a ___.

examples.why: Two different units compared.
A single measurement, not a comparison.

vocabulary.definition: A table of equal ratios that shows a pattern.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una tabla de razones iguales que muestra un patrón.
vocabulary.visual: Cups of juice: 2, 4, 6 | Cups of water: 3, 6, 9
vocabulary.cloze: A table that lists equivalent ratios in rows or columns is a ___.

examples.why: Every column holds the same ratio.
The last column breaks the pattern.

launch.narrative: Missed a lesson — or just want a refresher? This catch-up station reviews Lessons 3.1–3.3: 3.1 Understand Ratios, 3.2 Understand Rates and Unit Rates, 3.3 Determine Equivalent Ratios Using Tables. Read the Big Ideas, warm up with the review problem, then prove you're caught up in the mixed practice.

conceptIntro.heading: The Big Ideas — Lessons 3.1–3.3
conceptIntro.intro: Here is the one thing to remember from each lesson, plus a quick guided example. If one of these feels shaky, that lesson is right above this one in the menu — you can open it any time.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: 3.1: A ratio compares two quantities, and the order you write them in matters. You can write a ratio in words or with a colon, and you can draw it with a tape diagram or a double number line. • 3.2: To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of items. A unit rate that gives a cost is called a unit price, and the lower unit price is the better buy. • 3.3: To keep a ratio the same, multiply both numbers by the same scale factor.

iDo.title: The Big Ideas (one per lesson)
lines: Lesson 3.1 — Understand Ratios: A ratio compares two quantities, and the order you write them in matters. You can write a ratio in words or with a colon, and you can draw it with a tape diagram or a double number line.

Lesson 3.2 — Understand Rates and Unit Rates: To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of items. A unit rate that gives a cost is called a unit price, and the lower unit price is the better buy.
Lesson 3.3 — Determine Equivalent Ratios Using Tables: To keep a ratio the same, multiply both numbers by the same scale factor.

weDo.title: Quick guided checks — one from each lesson
lines: From 3.1: A bowl has 4 apples and 1 orange. What two amounts are we comparing?
From 3.2: A booth charges $4 for 8 games. What do we divide?
From 3.3: A drink uses 1 cup of juice for every 4 cups of water, so the ratio is 1:4.

youDo.title: Show you're caught up
lines: The practice below mixes problems from Lessons 3.1–3.3. Each problem is tagged with its lesson number.
Stuck on one lesson's problems? Open that lesson from the curriculum menu for the full re-teach.

diagram.kName: cups of milk per cup of mix

explore.instructions: Chef Reyes's pancake recipe uses 2 cups of mix for every 3 cups of milk. Complete the ratio table to scale the recipe for more students.

discourse.prompt: How did you find each new row in the pancake ratio table? If someone asked for 10 batches instead of 4, would counting up by adding 2 and 3 each row still be a fast way to find the answer?
discourse.sentenceFrame: I found the 4-batch row by multiplying ___ and ___ by ___, which is faster than adding ___ and ___ over and over ___ times.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.1) Prep Bowl A: Chef Reyes stirs 7 cups of flour with 4 cups of water to make dough. What is the part-to-part ratio of flour to water?
optional.explanation: Part-to-part compares the two ingredients in the order named. Flour to water = 7 to 4, written 7:4.
choiceFeedback: The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
You added the numbers together — a ratio compares two amounts, not their sum.
11 is the total number of cups, not an ingredient. Part-to-part compares the two ingredients themselves.
optional.stemEs: Tazón de preparación A: el chef Reyes mezcla 7 tazas de harina con 4 tazas de agua para hacer masa. ¿Cuál es la razón parte a parte de harina a agua?
optional.explanationEs: Parte a parte compara los dos ingredientes en el orden en que se nombran. Harina a agua = 7 a 4, escrito 7:4.
hints: A ratio compares two amounts in the exact order the question names them.
Part-to-part compares one ingredient directly to the other ingredient, so there is no total to add here.
The question names flour first, so 7 goes in the first spot — now decide which amount belongs after the colon.
hintsEs: Una razón compara dos cantidades en el mismo orden en que las nombra la pregunta.
Parte a parte compara un ingrediente directamente con el otro, así que aquí no hay que sumar ningún total.
La pregunta nombra primero la harina, así que el 7 va en el primer lugar; ahora decide qué cantidad va después de los dos puntos.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.2) The Star Blaster cabinet scored 90 points in 3 games. What is the unit rate in points per game?
optional.explanation: Divide points by games: 90 ÷ 3 = 30 points per game.
choiceFeedback: You found 90 × 3 — check: should you multiply or divide to find the rate for one game?
You picked 3 — is that the total points or the points for one game?
You found 90 + 3 — remember, a unit rate comes from dividing, not adding.
optional.stemEs: La máquina Star Blaster marcó 90 puntos en 3 juegos. ¿Cuál es la tasa por unidad en puntos por juego?
optional.explanationEs: Divide los puntos entre los juegos: 90 ÷ 3 = 30 puntos por juego.
hints: A unit rate tells you the amount for exactly one of something — here, for one game.
Divide the quantity named first (points) by the quantity named second (games).
Set up 90 ÷ 3 and think about how many 3s fit into 90.
hintsEs: Una tasa por unidad indica la cantidad que corresponde a exactamente uno: aquí, a un juego.
Divide la cantidad nombrada primero (puntos) entre la cantidad nombrada después (juegos).
Plantea 90 ÷ 3 y piensa cuántos 3 caben en 90.

optional.stem: (Lesson 3.3) The food truck sells tacos at a steady rate: 2 tacos cost $5. At that rate, how much do 6 tacos cost?
optional.explanation: 6 tacos is 3 times 2 tacos, so multiply the cost by 3: $5 x 3 = $15.
choiceFeedback: Figure out the unit rate first, then scale up correctly.
$12 doesn't come from scaling the price. First find 6 ÷ 2 to see what everything gets multiplied by.
You doubled it, but check if that's the right scale factor.
optional.stemEs: El camión de comida vende tacos a un ritmo constante: 2 tacos cuestan $5. A ese ritmo, ¿cuánto cuestan 6 tacos?
optional.explanationEs: 6 tacos son 3 veces 2 tacos, así que multiplica el costo por 3: $5 x 3 = $15.
hints: Tacos and cost grow together at the same rate, so this is a ratio table with two columns.
Find how many times bigger 6 tacos is than 2 tacos, then apply that same factor to the price.
6 ÷ 2 = 3, so the order is 3 times as big. Now scale the $5 by that same factor.
hintsEs: Los tacos y el costo crecen juntos al mismo ritmo, así que esto es una tabla de razones con dos columnas.
Halla cuántas veces más grande es 6 tacos que 2 tacos y aplica ese mismo factor al precio.
6 ÷ 2 = 3, así que el pedido es 3 veces más grande. Ahora escala los $5 con ese mismo factor.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.1) A recipe uses 4 cups of milk and 1 cup of cream. What is the ratio of milk to cream?
approaching.explanation: A ratio compares quantities in the order given. Milk to cream = 4 to 1, or 4:1.
choiceFeedback: The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
You added the numbers together — a ratio compares two amounts, not their sum.
5 is the total number of cups, not the amount of cream. This compares the whole recipe to one part instead of milk to cream.
hints: Re-read the question: it asks for milk to cream, in that exact order.
In a ratio, the amount named first goes first. Find the milk amount and the cream amount before you write anything.
Underline the two amounts: milk = 4 cups, cream = 1 cup. Write them in the same order the question names them.
approaching.stemEs: Una receta usa 4 tazas de leche y 1 taza de crema. ¿Cuál es la razón de leche a crema?
approaching.explanationEs: Una razón compara cantidades en el orden que se indica. Leche a crema = 4 a 1, o 4:1.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la pregunta: pide leche a crema, exactamente en ese orden.
En una razón, la cantidad que se nombra primero va primero. Halla la cantidad de leche y la de crema antes de escribir nada.
Subraya las dos cantidades: leche = 4 tazas, crema = 1 taza. Escríbelas en el mismo orden en que las nombra la pregunta.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.1) Chef Reyes uses 6 strawberries and 2 bananas in a smoothie. What is the part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit?
approaching.explanation: Total fruit = 6 + 2 = 8. The part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit is 2:8.
choiceFeedback: Re-check: does this show a part being compared to the whole group?
This compares bananas to strawberries, which is part-to-part. A part-to-whole ratio needs the total number of pieces of fruit as the second number.
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
hints: Notice the word 'total' — this is a part-to-WHOLE ratio, not banana-to-strawberry.
First find the total fruit by adding strawberries and bananas. Then compare bananas to that total.
Add 6 + 2 to get the total fruit. Then write the bananas' number first, followed by that total.
approaching.stemEs: El chef Reyes usa 6 fresas y 2 plátanos en un batido. ¿Cuál es la razón parte a todo de plátanos a fruta total?
approaching.explanationEs: Fruta total = 6 + 2 = 8. La razón parte a todo de plátanos a fruta total es 2:8.
hintsEs: Fíjate en la palabra 'total': esta es una razón parte a TODO, no de plátano a fresa.
Primero halla la fruta total sumando las fresas y los plátanos. Luego compara los plátanos con ese total.
Suma 6 + 2 para obtener la fruta total. Luego escribe primero el número de plátanos, seguido de ese total.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.2) A booth charges $4.50 for 9 games. What is the unit rate?
choiceFeedback: Double-check your division: $4.50 ÷ 9 — is it $0.45 or $0.50?
Divide the cost by the number of games: $4.50 ÷ 9, not some other operation.
That's the total cost for all 9 games, not the cost for one game.
hints: You know the total cost ($4.50) and the total games (9). A unit rate tells the cost of just ONE game.
To find a unit rate, divide the total cost by the number of games so the second quantity becomes 1.
Set up the division: $4.50 ÷ 9. Think of $4.50 as 450 cents if that makes the division easier.
approaching.stemEs: Un puesto cobra $4.50 por 9 juegos. ¿Cuál es la tasa por unidad?
hintsEs: Conoces el costo total ($4.50) y el total de juegos (9). Una tasa unitaria dice el costo de UN solo juego.
Para hallar una tasa unitaria, divide el costo total entre el número de juegos para que la segunda cantidad sea 1.
Plantea la división: $4.50 ÷ 9. Piensa en $4.50 como 450 centavos si eso te facilita la división.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.2) A car travels 180 miles using 6 gallons of gas. What is the unit rate in miles per gallon?
choiceFeedback: That's the number of gallons — you need to divide 180 by 6, not use 6 as the answer.
That's the total miles — divide 180 by 6 to find miles for one gallon.
Check your division: 180 ÷ 6 — is it 30 or 36?
hints: Notice the units in the question: miles PER gallon. That tells you miles go on top and gallons on the bottom.
Divide the total miles by the total gallons so you get the miles for just 1 gallon.
Start the division: 180 ÷ 6. Think: 6 × what number lands on 180?
approaching.stemEs: Un carro recorre 180 millas usando 6 galones de gasolina. ¿Cuál es la tasa por unidad en millas por galón?
hintsEs: Fíjate en las unidades de la pregunta: millas POR galón. Eso te dice que las millas van arriba y los galones abajo.
Divide el total de millas entre el total de galones para obtener las millas de 1 solo galón.
Empieza la división: 180 ÷ 6. Piensa: 6 × ¿qué número da 180?

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.3) A recipe uses 3 eggs for every 5 cups of flour. How many eggs are needed for 15 cups of flour?
approaching.explanation: The scale factor is 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Multiply the eggs by 3: 3 × 3 = 9 eggs.
choiceFeedback: Re-check how many times you need to multiply or scale.
10 doesn't come from scaling the egg row. Find the factor with 15 ÷ 5 and apply it to the 3, not the 5.
It looks like you multiplied by 4 instead of 3. Check the factor: 15 ÷ 5 tells you how many times the table grows.
hints: Notice the flour jumped from 5 cups to 15 cups — the eggs must grow by the same factor.
Find the scale factor by dividing the new flour by the recipe's flour, then multiply the eggs by that same factor.
Divide 15 ÷ 5 to get the scale factor. Then multiply 3 eggs by that factor to scale the recipe.
approaching.stemEs: Una receta usa 3 huevos por cada 5 tazas de harina. ¿Cuántos huevos se necesitan para 15 tazas de harina?
approaching.explanationEs: El factor de escala es 15 ÷ 5 = 3. Multiplica los huevos por 3: 3 × 3 = 9 huevos.
hintsEs: Fíjate que la harina pasó de 5 tazas a 15 tazas: los huevos deben crecer con el mismo factor.
Halla el factor de escala dividiendo la harina nueva entre la harina de la receta y luego multiplica los huevos por ese mismo factor.
Divide 15 ÷ 5 para obtener el factor de escala. Luego multiplica los 3 huevos por ese factor para escalar la receta.

approaching.stem: (Lesson 3.3) Which row does NOT belong in a ratio table for 4:5?
approaching.explanation: 6:10 simplifies to 3:5, not 4:5. The other ratios (8:10, 12:15, 16:20) all simplify to 4:5.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. simplifies to 3:5, not 4:5.
You doubled it, but check if that's the right scale factor.
16:20 DOES belong in the table: dividing both numbers by 4 gives 4:5. Simplify each option and find the one that does not give 4:5.
hints: Every row in a 4:5 table must simplify back to exactly 4:5.
For each choice, ask: can I multiply 4 AND 5 by the same number to get these two values? Check both parts, not just one.
Work through the choices in order. For each one ask: is there a single number that multiplies BOTH 4 and 5 into these two values?
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál fila NO pertenece a una tabla de razones de 4:5?
approaching.explanationEs: 6:10 se simplifica a 3:5, no a 4:5. Las demás razones (8:10, 12:15, 16:20) se simplifican todas a 4:5.
hintsEs: Cada fila de una tabla 4:5 debe simplificarse exactamente a 4:5.
Para cada opción pregunta: ¿puedo multiplicar el 4 Y el 5 por el mismo número para obtener esos dos valores? Revisa ambas partes, no solo una.
Prueba la primera opción, 6:10: ¿por cuánto multiplicas el 4 para obtener 6? ¿Multiplicar el 5 por ese mismo número da 10?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.1) A fruit salad has 5 pieces of melon, 3 pieces of pineapple, and 2 grapes. What is the ratio of pineapple to melon?
onLevel.explanation: The ratio of pineapple to melon compares pineapple (3) to melon (5), so the ratio is 3:5.
choiceFeedback: The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
That compares pineapple to the total (5 + 3 + 2). The question compares pineapple to melon only.
You started with the pineapple, which fits the order — but 2 is the number of grapes. Re-read which two amounts the question compares.
hints: Three fruits are listed, but the question only compares pineapple and melon — the grapes are extra info.
Pick out just the two amounts you need, then write them in the order the question names: pineapple first.
Circle the pineapple count (3) and the melon count (5). Write them in the order 'pineapple to melon.'
onLevel.stemEs: Una ensalada de frutas tiene 5 trozos de melón, 3 trozos de piña y 2 uvas. ¿Cuál es la razón de piña a melón?
onLevel.explanationEs: La razón de piña a melón compara la piña (3) con el melón (5), así que la razón es 3:5.
hintsEs: Se mencionan tres frutas, pero la pregunta solo compara piña y melón — las uvas son información de más.
Escoge solo las dos cantidades que necesitas y escríbelas en el orden que nombra la pregunta: la piña primero.
Encierra la cantidad de piña (3) y la de melón (5). Escríbelas en el orden 'piña a melón'.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.1) A parking lot has 10 cars and 6 trucks. What is the part-to-whole ratio of trucks to total vehicles?
onLevel.explanation: Total vehicles = 10 + 6 = 16. The ratio of trucks to total is 6:16.
choiceFeedback: Re-check: does this show a part being compared to the whole group?
This compares trucks to cars, which is a part-to-part ratio. For part-to-whole you need 10 + 6 as the second number.
The order matters — what is named first should be first in the ratio.
hints: The word 'total' means this is part-to-whole — compare trucks to ALL vehicles, not to cars.
First find the total number of vehicles by adding cars and trucks. The trucks' number goes first.
Add 10 + 6 to find the total vehicles. Then write 6 (the trucks) first and that total second.
onLevel.stemEs: Un estacionamiento tiene 10 autos y 6 camionetas. ¿Cuál es la razón parte a todo de camionetas al total de vehículos?
onLevel.explanationEs: Total de vehículos = 10 + 6 = 16. La razón de camionetas al total es 6:16.
hintsEs: La palabra 'total' significa que esto es parte a todo: compara los camiones con TODOS los vehículos, no con los carros.
Primero halla el número total de vehículos sumando carros y camiones. El número de camiones va primero.
Suma 10 + 6 para hallar el total de vehículos. Luego escribe 6 (los camiones) primero y ese total después.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.2) Which token pack from the table above is the best deal?
onLevel.explanation: Pack B has a unit rate of $0.20 per token, which is the lowest cost per token.
choiceFeedback: Compare the cost per token, not the total price or the total number of tokens. Divide each pack's price by its tokens and compare those results.
A bigger pack is not automatically cheaper for each token. Work out price ÷ tokens for every pack before deciding.
Compare the unit rates: $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25. Are all three the same?
hints: The 'best deal' is the pack where ONE token costs the least — not the pack with the most tokens.
Line up the three unit rates you found in the table and look for the smallest cost per token.
Compare $0.25, $0.20, and $0.25 per token. Which of those is the smallest amount of money?
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál paquete de fichas de la tabla de arriba es la mejor oferta?
onLevel.explanationEs: El paquete B tiene una tasa por unidad de $0.20 por ficha, que es el menor costo por ficha.
hintsEs: La 'mejor oferta' es el paquete donde UNA ficha cuesta menos — no el paquete con más fichas.
Alinea las tres tasas unitarias que hallaste en la tabla y busca el menor costo por ficha.
Compara $0.25, $0.20 y $0.25 por ficha. ¿Cuál de esos es la menor cantidad de dinero?

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.2) Runner A completes 4 laps in 12 minutes. Runner B completes 5 laps in 14 minutes. Who runs more laps per minute?
onLevel.explanation: Runner A: 4÷12 ≈ 0.33 laps/min. Runner B: 5÷14 ≈ 0.36 laps/min. Runner B runs slightly more laps per minute.
choiceFeedback: You found 4 ÷ 12, but compare: is 0.33 laps per minute more or less than 0.36?
Divide each runner's laps by their minutes. You should get two different rates.
You have the laps and the minutes for both runners — that's enough to find and compare their rates.
hints: Each runner has laps and minutes. 'More laps per minute' means you need each runner's laps-per-minute rate first.
Divide laps by minutes for BOTH runners, then compare the two decimals — bigger decimal means faster.
Start with Runner A: 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 laps per minute. Now find Runner B's rate with 5 ÷ 14 and compare.
onLevel.stemEs: El corredor A completa 4 vueltas en 12 minutos. El corredor B completa 5 vueltas en 14 minutos. ¿Quién da más vueltas por minuto?
onLevel.explanationEs: Corredor A: 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 vueltas/min. Corredor B: 5 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.36 vueltas/min. El corredor B da un poco más de vueltas por minuto.
hintsEs: Cada corredor tiene vueltas y minutos. 'Más vueltas por minuto' significa que primero necesitas la tasa de vueltas por minuto de cada uno.
Divide vueltas entre minutos para AMBOS corredores y luego compara los dos decimales: mayor decimal significa más rápido.
Empieza con el Corredor A: 4 ÷ 12 ≈ 0.33 vueltas por minuto. Ahora halla la tasa del Corredor B con 5 ÷ 14 y compara.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.3) In a ratio table, the ratio of sugar to butter is 3:2. If you use 12 cups of sugar, how many cups of butter do you need?
onLevel.explanation: Scale factor: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Multiply butter by 4: 2 × 4 = 8 cups of butter.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. Scale factor: 12 ÷ 3 = ___.
10 doesn't come from scaling the butter. Find the factor with 12 ÷ 3, then apply it to the 2.
It looks like you subtracted 12 − 3 instead of scaling. Multiply the butter by the same factor you used for the sugar.
hints: The sugar grew from 3 cups to 12 cups. The butter has to keep up with the same jump.
Divide the new sugar by the recipe's sugar to find the scale factor, then multiply the butter (2 cups) by it.
Divide 12 ÷ 3 to get the scale factor — then multiply 2 cups of butter by that number.
onLevel.stemEs: En una tabla de razones, la razón de azúcar a mantequilla es 3:2. Si usas 12 tazas de azúcar, ¿cuántas tazas de mantequilla necesitas?
onLevel.explanationEs: Factor de escala: 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Multiplica la mantequilla por 4: 2 × 4 = 8 tazas de mantequilla.
hintsEs: El azúcar pasó de 3 tazas a 12 tazas. La mantequilla tiene que seguir el mismo salto.
Divide el azúcar nuevo entre el azúcar de la receta para hallar el factor de escala y luego multiplica la mantequilla (2 tazas) por él.
Divide 12 ÷ 3 para obtener el factor de escala y luego multiplica 2 tazas de mantequilla por ese número.

onLevel.stem: (Lesson 3.3) A ratio table shows 5:8, 10:16, 15:24. What scale factor was used from the first row to the third row?
onLevel.explanation: From 5 to 15: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. From 8 to 24: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. The scale factor is 3.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. From 5 to 15: 15 ÷ 5 = ___.
5 is the first value of the ratio, not the scale factor. The factor comes from dividing 15 by 5.
8 is the second value of the original ratio, not the factor. Divide a value in the third row by the matching value in the first row.
hints: Compare the first row (5:8) with the third row (15:24). The question asks what number multiplies row 1 into row 3.
Divide a third-row value by its matching first-row value — and check the same number works for BOTH columns.
Divide 15 ÷ 5. Then confirm with the other column: does 24 ÷ 8 give the same number?
onLevel.stemEs: Una tabla de razones muestra 5:8, 10:16 y 15:24. ¿Qué factor de escala se usó de la primera fila a la tercera fila?
onLevel.explanationEs: De 5 a 15: 15 ÷ 5 = 3. De 8 a 24: 24 ÷ 8 = 3. El factor de escala es 3.
hintsEs: Compara la primera fila (5:8) con la tercera (15:24). La pregunta es qué número multiplica la fila 1 para dar la fila 3.
Divide un valor de la tercera fila entre el valor correspondiente de la primera, y revisa que el mismo número sirva para AMBAS columnas.
Divide 15 ÷ 5. Luego confirma con la otra columna: ¿24 ÷ 8 da el mismo número?

extending.title: (Lesson 3.1) Find Aliya's Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: A trail mix has 6 almonds, 4 raisins, and 2 cashews. Write the ratio of raisins to total pieces.
workedExample.workEs: Una mezcla de frutos secos tiene 6 almendras, 4 pasas y 2 anacardos. Escribe la razón de pasas al total de piezas.

workedExample.label: Answer
workedExample.work: The ratio of raisins to total is 4:8.
workedExample.workEs: La razón de pasas al total es 4:8.

extending.correctWork: The total is 12, not 8. The correct ratio is 4:12.
hints: Look at Step 3. Does 8 match the total Aliya found in Step 2?
The total is 12 pieces, so the part-to-whole ratio should use 12, not 8.
extending.explanation: Aliya counted the total correctly: 6 + 4 + 2 = 12 pieces. But the ratio she wrote uses 8, which is not the total — it is only the almonds and raisins together. Comparing the 4 raisins to the whole 12 pieces gives 4:12.
extending.explanationEs: Aliya contó bien el total: 6 + 4 + 2 = 12 piezas. Pero la razón que escribió usa 8, que no es el total: son solo las almendras y las pasas juntas. Comparar las 4 pasas con las 12 piezas completas da 4:12.
extending.correctWorkEs: El total es 12, no 8. La razón correcta es 4:12.
hintsEs: Mira el Paso 3. ¿8 coincide con el total que halló Aliya en el Paso 2?
El total son 12 piezas, así que la razón parte-a-todo debe usar 12, no 8.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.2) Find the Rate Error

workedExample.label: Find the unit rate: 12 tickets for $8
workedExample.labelEs: Encuentra la tasa unitaria: 12 boletos por $8

workedExample.label: Write the unit rate
workedExample.work: The unit rate is $1.50 per ticket
workedExample.workEs: La tasa unitaria es $1.50 por boleto

extending.correctWork: To find cost per ticket, divide $8 ÷ 12 = $0.67 per ticket (rounded). The student divided tickets by cost instead of cost by tickets.
hints: What should go in the numerator — the cost or the tickets?
To find 'dollars per ticket,' divide dollars by tickets: $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 per ticket.
extending.titleEs: Encuentra el error de la tasa
extending.explanation: The two quantities were divided in the wrong order. "Dollars per ticket" puts dollars on top, so the correct division is $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 per ticket. The student's 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 answers a different question, and $1.50 per ticket would mean 12 tickets cost $18 instead of $8.
extending.explanationEs: Las dos cantidades se dividieron en el orden equivocado. "Dólares por boleto" pone los dólares arriba, así que la división correcta es $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 por boleto. El 12 ÷ 8 = 1.5 del estudiante responde otra pregunta, y $1.50 por boleto significaría que 12 boletos cuestan $18 en lugar de $8.
extending.correctWorkEs: Para encontrar el costo por boleto, divide $8 ÷ 12 = $0.67 por boleto (redondeado). El estudiante dividió boletos entre costo en lugar de costo entre boletos.
hintsEs: ¿Qué debe ir en el numerador — el costo o los boletos?
Para hallar 'dólares por boleto', divide los dólares entre los boletos: $8 ÷ 12 ≈ $0.67 por boleto.

extending.title: (Lesson 3.3) Find Devon's Mistake

workedExample.label: Read the problem
workedExample.work: A recipe uses 5 cups of oats for every 2 cups of honey. Complete the table for 3 batches.
workedExample.workEs: Una receta usa 5 tazas de avena por cada 2 tazas de miel. Completa la tabla para 3 tandas.

extending.correctWork: 2 × 3 = 6 cups of honey (multiply, don't add the scale factor)
hints: Look at Step 4. Devon used a different operation for honey than for oats.
To keep the ratio equivalent, you must multiply BOTH quantities by the same scale factor.
extending.explanation: Devon multiplied the oats by the scale factor (5 × 3 = 15) but switched to addition for the honey (2 + 3 = 5). Both quantities have to use the same operation and the same scale factor, so the honey is 2 × 3 = 6 cups.
extending.explanationEs: Devon multiplicó la avena por el factor de escala (5 × 3 = 15), pero cambió a la suma para la miel (2 + 3 = 5). Las dos cantidades deben usar la misma operación y el mismo factor de escala, así que la miel es 2 × 3 = 6 tazas.
extending.correctWorkEs: 2 × 3 = 6 tazas de miel (multiplica, no sumes el factor de escala)
hintsEs: Mira el Paso 4. Devon usó una operación distinta para la miel que para la avena.
Para mantener la razón equivalente, debes multiplicar AMBAS cantidades por el mismo factor de escala.

optionalActivity.name: Catch-Up Challenge
optionalActivity.intro: Mix it up: pick the right lesson's big idea for each problem — that's the real catch-up skill.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Ratio Tables is scaling only ONE part of the ratio, or adding the scale factor to a part instead of multiplying by it — for example, turning 2:3 into 6:3 (multiplying only the first number by 3 and forgetting the second) or into 4:5 (adding the scale factor 2 to the second number instead of multiplying, since 3+2=5 but 3×2=6). Before you submit, multiply BOTH numbers by the same scale factor and check that your new ratio simplifies back to the original.

simulator.title: Fill the ratio table (5 miles per hour)

diagram.title: Berry Blast Smoothie Ratio
diagram.caption: Each serving uses 3 berry parts for 2 yogurt parts; multiply both rows by the same scale factor to fill the ratio table for 20 people.

connect.scenario: A juice bar makes a Berry Blast smoothie with 3 scoops of frozen berries for every 2 cups of yogurt. A customer orders enough for a party of 20 people, and each person gets one serving. The juice bar needs to use a ratio table to figure out how many scoops and cups to prepare.
connect.prompt: The recipe uses 3 scoops of berries for every ___ cups of yogurt, so 20 servings need ___ scoops of berries and ___ cups of yogurt.

check.stem: One serving uses 3 scoops of berries and 2 cups of yogurt. How many scoops for 20 servings?
check.explanation: Multiply both parts of the ratio by the same scale factor of 20: 3 × 20 = 60 scoops.

check.stem: How many cups of yogurt are needed for 20 servings?
check.explanation: 2 × 20 = 40 cups. Both rows of the ratio table grow by the same factor.

check.stem: Which pair is NOT equivalent to 3:2?
check.explanation: 9:6, 6:4 and 30:20 all simplify to 3:2. 5:4 does not — you cannot reach it by multiplying 3 and 2 by the same number.

connect.modelAnswer: A ratio table grows by multiplying both rows by the same scale factor. For 20 servings the factor is 20, so the juice bar needs 3 × 20 = 60 scoops of berries and 2 × 20 = 40 cups of yogurt. The ratio 60:40 still simplifies to 3:2, so the smoothie tastes the same.

exitTicket.stem: (Catch-up check, from Lesson 3.2) A store sells 6 pencils for $1.50 and 10 pencils for $2.80. Which is the better buy?
choices: They cost the same per pencil
exitTicket.explanation: $1.50 ÷ 6 = $0.25 per pencil. $2.80 ÷ 10 = $0.28 per pencil. $0.25 < $0.28, so 6 for $1.50 is the better buy.
choiceFeedback: You found the unit rates, but which one is lower — $0.25 or $0.28?
Divide the cost by the number for each pack. You should get $0.25 and $0.28.
You have the cost and quantity for both packs — that's enough to find and compare unit rates.
hints: Better buy means the lower cost for ONE pencil — you can't compare $1.50 and $2.80 directly because the packs have different counts.
Find each pack's unit price: divide the price by the number of pencils, then compare the two per-pencil costs.
Start with the first pack: $1.50 ÷ 6 pencils. Then compute $2.80 ÷ 10 and pick the smaller per-pencil price.

questions.stem: In a class of 30 students, 18 are girls. What is the part-to-part ratio of boys to girls?
questions.explanation: Boys = 30 − 18 = 12. Part-to-part ratio of boys to girls = 12:18. (Order matters!)

questions.stem: A recipe uses 4 cups of milk and 1 cup of cream. What is the ratio of milk to cream?
questions.explanation: A ratio compares quantities in the order given. Milk to cream = 4 to 1, or 4:1.

questions.stem: Chef Reyes uses 6 strawberries and 2 bananas in a smoothie. What is the part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit?
questions.explanation: Total fruit = 6 + 2 = 8. The part-to-whole ratio of bananas to total fruit is 2:8.
